# Weak Traits Are Self-Maintaining

## Nobody Practises Being Petty

Think about the qualities you like in yourself. Generosity, maybe. Patience with people who are slow. The ability to stay steady when something goes wrong.

Now think about when you last had them reliably.

For most people the honest answer is *not recently*, and there is usually a reason available — a bad year, too much work, a period where everything was difficult. The reason is probably true.

Now do the same exercise with the qualities you do not like in yourself. The impatience. The tendency to go cold when criticized. The thing you do when you are cornered.

**Those have not required a good year.** They did not lapse during the difficult period. They have been available, at full strength, the entire time, without a single day of maintenance.

Greene states the asymmetry in one sentence and it is the most quietly disturbing claim in the chapter:

> **The weakest parts of our character are the ones that create habits and compulsive behaviour, because they do not require effort or practice to maintain.**[^1]

## The Full Statement

The passage is short and worth having in its parts, because each clause is doing work.

**Some character traits are positive and reflect inner strength** — a propensity toward being generous and open, empathetic, resilient under pressure.

**But these stronger, more flexible qualities often require awareness and practice to truly become habits that can be relied upon.**[^1]

Note what that does to the word *strength*. It is not describing something you have. It is describing something you are currently maintaining, and the maintenance is conditional on attention.

Then the direction of drift: **as we get older, life tends to weaken us.** Empathy becomes harder to hold onto.[^1]

Then two specific decay paths, and they are more interesting than general decline because each shows a strength becoming its own failure mode.

**Generosity, unmaintained, becomes indiscriminate**: if we are reflexively generous and open to everyone we meet, **we can end up in a lot of trouble.** The trait has not weakened — it has lost its discrimination, which is the part that required attention.

**Confidence, unmaintained, becomes grandiosity**: confidence without self-awareness and control.[^1]

So the mechanism is not that strengths fade to zero. **They lose the governor.** Generosity plus judgment is a strength; generosity minus judgment is a vulnerability wearing the same name. And the judgment is the expensive component.

Greene's conclusion: **without conscious effort, these strengths will tend to wear down or turn into weaknesses.**[^1]

## Why the Asymmetry Exists

Greene does not spell out the mechanism, but it follows directly from his own account of character in the same chapter, and assembling it makes the claim much harder to dismiss.

He describes a decision as **engraved neurologically**, creating a path — and we are compelled to repeat it **because the path is already laid.**[^2]

A weak trait is a laid path. Nothing has to be done to keep a path open; **it is the default route, and defaults require no upkeep by definition.** Going that way is not a choice you make. It is what happens when no choice is made.

A strength, on the other hand, is an *override*. It is the thing you do instead of the default, which means every instance requires the override to fire. And overrides run on attention, which is finite, contested, and the first thing to go under load.

Which explains the specific timing everyone recognizes. **Your worst traits appear exactly when you are tired, stressed, rushed, or ill** — not because those conditions make you a worse person, but because they are the conditions in which the override budget is spent and the default is all that remains.

That is the same finding Greene reaches from the other direction elsewhere in the book: **stress or tension can reveal flaws in people that they have carefully concealed from view**,[^3] and **never imagine that you are someone who can withstand rising stress without emotional leakage. It is not possible.**[^3]

Stress does not add the flaw. **It withdraws the funding from the correction.**

## Analytical Case Study: Entropy With a Direction

Set this beside the ordinary way people think about self-improvement, because the difference is practical rather than philosophical.

The common model is a balance: you have good qualities and bad ones, you work on the bad ones, and over time the ratio improves. Improvement is cumulative. Progress is held.

Greene's model has **no holding.** The good qualities require continuous expenditure and the bad ones are free — so the resting state of any unattended character is **not neutral. It is the worst version of itself**, and it arrives without anybody doing anything.

Which reframes what maintenance means. **Not doing the work is not staying still; it is moving**, in a specific direction, at a rate set by how much load you are under.

And it explains a phenomenon that otherwise looks like hypocrisy. People who genuinely improve some quality — patience, say — and then lose it entirely two years later are not frauds and did not backslide through weakness. **They stopped paying, and the trait was never owned.**

Greene's whole chapter is built on this. His account of why compulsive behaviour is compulsive is not that the weak trait is unusually strong. It is that **it is the only part of the character that runs unattended** — so over a life, it accumulates far more instances than any strength, and each instance deepens the path that makes the next one easier.[^2]

**The strong trait and the weak trait are not competing on merit. They are competing on running cost, and one of them is free.**

## What the Maintenance Actually Is

If strengths need practice, the obvious question is what the practice consists of. Greene supplies a list in the chapter's closing section, and it is unusually concrete for this book.

**Train yourself to not react in the moment by repeatedly placing yourself in stressful or adverse situations in order to get used to them.**[^4]

That is graded exposure, and note that it is not introspective. You do not become less reactive by understanding your reactivity; you become less reactive by being in the situation often enough that it stops being novel.

**In boring everyday tasks, cultivate greater patience and attention to detail.**[^4]

The word *boring* is load-bearing. Patience practised only where it matters is not practised at all, because the occasions are too rare to build anything.

**Deliberately take on tasks slightly above your level.** In completing them you have to work harder, **helping you establish more discipline and better work habits.**[^4]

*Slightly* is the design constraint. Far above your level produces failure and avoidance; at your level produces nothing.

**Train yourself to continually think of what is best for the team.**[^4]

**Search out others who display strong character and associate with them as much as possible**, so as to **assimilate their energy and their habits.**[^4]

That one is environmental rather than personal, and it is the highest-leverage item on the list precisely because it does not run on your own attention budget. **Proximity does the maintenance for you.**

**And to develop flexibility — always a sign of strength — occasionally shake yourself up, trying some new strategy or doing the opposite of what you would normally do.**[^4]

Greene's summary of what all six have in common: **the only way to do so is to work on your habits, which go into the slow formation of your character.**[^4]

Habits, not insight. Which is the correct implication of his own mechanism and one he does not always follow elsewhere.

## The Consequence for Judging Others

This page has a diagnostic application that Greene draws out in the neighbouring material, and it is worth stating because it changes how a record should be read.

**Weak character neutralizes all of the other possible good qualities a person might possess.**[^5]

Someone of high intelligence but weak character may produce good ideas and even do a job well — **and they will crumble under pressure, or not take kindly to criticism, or think first of their own agenda, or their arrogance will cause others around them to quit.** Greene calls these **hidden costs.**[^5]

The asymmetry explains why. Intelligence is not maintained by effort; it is largely available regardless of load. **So a person's intelligence shows up in every sample and their strength of character shows up only in samples taken under load** — which are rare, unscheduled, and exactly the ones an interview does not contain.

Which means an evaluation built from ordinary interactions is systematically biased toward the free traits. **You are measuring, with high reliability, precisely the qualities that do not fail** — and inferring from them the qualities that do.

Greene's conclusion follows: **someone less charming and intelligent but of strong character will prove more reliable and productive over the long run. People of real strength are as rare as gold.**[^5]

## The Third Option

There is a way out of the maintenance problem that Greene supplies at the end of the chapter, and it is better than either denial or perpetual upkeep.

**You see your character as the clay that you will work with, slowly transforming your very weaknesses into strengths. You do not run away from your flaws but rather see them as a true source of power.**[^6]

That is a different operation from maintaining a strength, and the difference is economic. Maintenance means running an override against a default, forever, on an attention budget. **Conversion means pointing the default at something where its shape is useful** — at which point it costs nothing, because you are no longer fighting it.

Greene's worked examples make the mechanism concrete, and each pairs a specific flaw with its specific corresponding strength.

**A hyperperfectionist who likes to control everything** must redirect that energy **into some productive work instead of using it on people.** The attention to detail and high standards are a positive **if you channel them correctly.**

**A pleaser** has developed courtier skills and real charm; seeing the source of the trait lets you control the compulsive and defensive aspect **and use it as a genuine social skill that can bring you great power.**

**Someone highly sensitive and prone to take things personally** can redirect that into **active empathy**, converting the flaw into an asset for social purposes.

**A rebellious character** has a natural dislike of conventions and usual ways of doing things — which channels into **innovative work, instead of compulsively insulting and alienating people.**[^6]

And the principle: **for each weakness there is a corresponding strength.**[^6]

The reason this beats maintenance is not that it is easier to start. It is that **it does not deplete.** The hyperperfectionist pointed at a manuscript instead of at a team is not exercising restraint; they are doing the thing they were always going to do, in a place where it produces something. There is no override to fund, so a bad week does not undo it.

Which suggests the correct order of operations, and it is not the one most people run. **Convert what can be converted, and reserve the expensive maintenance budget for the few qualities that have no useful channel** — because that budget is small, it empties under load, and most people spend all of it fighting traits that could have been redirected instead.

## Implementation Workflow

You want to know which of your strengths is currently unfunded.

**Do not ask which qualities you value.** Ask this instead: **what did the last genuinely bad week look like?**

Pick a real one — a fortnight where you were overloaded, or something went wrong at home, or you were ill. Then list, specifically, what you did *not* do during it.

You will find the unfunded strengths immediately, because they are the ones that disappeared. Perhaps you stopped asking colleagues how they were. Perhaps you stopped reading anything. Perhaps the person you are careful with stopped getting the care.

**That list is your maintenance schedule**, and it is more accurate than any values exercise, because it was generated by an actual stress test rather than by a preference.

**Now pick one and make it cheap.** The reason strengths lapse under load is that they run on attention, so anything requiring a decision will fail in exactly the conditions where it is needed. Attach it to something that already happens: the question gets asked at the start of every one-to-one because it is the first line of the agenda, not because you remembered.

**Then build the one thing on Greene's list that does not cost attention.** Proximity.[^4] Who do you spend time with who is reliably steady under pressure, patient in tedium, or straightforward when something goes wrong? If the honest answer is nobody, that is the finding — and it is the highest-leverage one, because every other item on the list depletes and this one does not.

**And run the graded exposure deliberately rather than waiting for it.** Greene's instruction is to place yourself in stressful situations repeatedly to get used to them.[^4] In practice: the conversation you have been putting off for three weeks is the training, and having it is worth more than the outcome of it. Take the task slightly above your level, on purpose, this quarter.

**Finally, and this is the part that follows from the asymmetry:** stop expecting to arrive. There is no state in which the strength is secured and the maintenance can stop. Greene's model has no such state — **without conscious effort, these strengths will tend to wear down or turn into weaknesses.**[^1] The correct relationship to a good quality of yours is the one you have with fitness, not the one you have with a qualification.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

This is a single paragraph of assertion.[^1] Greene supplies no study, no case, and no mechanism — the neurological account has to be borrowed from elsewhere in his own chapter to make it coherent. 🚩 SINGLE SOURCE; `[POPULAR SOURCE]`. The underlying idea has real relatives in the habit and self-regulation literature (ego depletion in particular), and it is worth noting that **ego depletion is one of the more prominently failed replications of the last decade** — so the most obvious empirical support for this page is `[CONTESTED]` and should not be leaned on.

**The load-bearing tension is that the claim is stated as universal and is probably not.** Some good qualities do appear to become genuinely automatic — people raised in certain ways are reflexively honest under pressure, and it costs them nothing. Greene's model has no room for a strength that becomes a default, yet his own framework describes exactly the mechanism by which one would: **a path laid by enough repetition is a path.**[^2]

Which suggests the real claim is narrower and more useful: **strengths are expensive until they are engraved, and most people never repeat them enough to engrave them.** That preserves the practical advice and removes the fatalism, and it also explains the observation the strong version cannot — that some people really are dependably decent when tired.

**Second tension: the framework licenses a comfortable excuse.** "My worst self appears under stress because the correction is unfunded" is true and is also available as an explanation for behaviour that hurt someone. The mechanism explains; it does not excuse, and Greene's own instruction is that the training happens *by* repeatedly entering the stressful situation.[^4] **A person whose bad behaviour only ever appears under load has not discovered a limit on human nature. They have discovered where their practice needs to be.**

**Open question:** the highest-leverage item on Greene's list is proximity to strong characters, because it is the only one that does not consume the reader's own attention.[^4] But the mechanism by which proximity works is not stated — assimilation of energy and habits is a description, not an explanation. If it works by making the strong behaviour the local default, then this is the *environmental* intervention the chapter's own neurology implies and its prescriptions otherwise avoid. Is character maintenance therefore mostly a question of who you are near, and is the introspective programme largely beside the point?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/character-as-engraving|Character as Engraving]] supplies the mechanism this page needs and does not state, and reading them together resolves the apparent paradox of the layered model.

If character is laid down as paths, then everything on this page follows without further assumption: the deepest and most-travelled paths are the ones formed earliest and used most, defaults require no maintenance, and overrides do. **The asymmetry is not an additional claim about strengths and weaknesses. It is what the engraving model predicts.**

And it exposes something the engraving page leaves implicit. Greene's four layers are not equally weighted in ordinary operation — **the deepest layers win by default under any condition where the shallower ones are not being actively run.** Which means "character under stress" is not a distortion of someone's real character. It is the lower layers with the upper ones temporarily unfunded.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/strong-and-weak-character|Strong and Weak Character]] converges on the diagnostic consequence. That page's tensile-strength account describes what a maintained character looks like; this one explains why so few people have one. **Strength being rare is not a claim about human quality. It is an arithmetic consequence of one option being free.**

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**→ [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/trait-development-composure-charisma|Trait Development: Composure and Charisma]]**

This is the mandatory psychology-to-behavioral-mechanics handshake, and the operational corpus supplies exactly what Greene's paragraph lacks: **a curriculum.**

That page treats composure as a trainable trait with specified drills, rather than as a quality someone has. Which is the same underlying claim as this page — the trait is maintained rather than possessed — but arrived at from the practitioner's side, where the question was never *why do people lose it* but *how do we install it.*

The insight the pairing produces concerns **what the practitioner literature knows that the psychological literature does not: the maintenance has to be scheduled rather than intended.**

Greene's prescriptions are all things a reader is supposed to *do more of* — be more patient in tedious tasks, take on harder work, think of the team.[^4] Every one of those is an intention, and intentions are precisely the thing that fails under load, which is the condition this page says the traits fail in. **The advice is denominated in the currency it has just told you will run out.**

The operational version does not rely on intention at all. It specifies a rep, a frequency, and a condition — and the whole point is that the drill continues on a bad week because it is on the schedule rather than because the operator felt like it.

**Which supplies the correction: any character-maintenance programme that requires you to remember it will fail on exactly the days it exists for.** The only versions that survive are the ones attached to something that happens anyway — a recurring meeting, a standing commitment, a person who will notice. Greene's own list contains one item of that kind, proximity to strong characters, and he does not mark it as different in kind from the other five.

**→ [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/hours-not-minutes-the-discipline-of-japa|Hours Not Minutes: The Discipline of Japa]]**

The contemplative traditions arrived at this page's asymmetry a very long time ago, from practice rather than from theory, and their conclusion is more demanding than Greene's.

That material holds that practice must be **daily and substantial** — that a discipline done occasionally is not a diluted version of a discipline done daily but a different thing that does not work, and that the quantity is not negotiable downward.

Which is a strange requirement unless you already believe something like this page's claim. **If practice were cumulative and gains were held, occasional practice would produce slow progress.** The insistence on dailiness only makes sense if the untended state is not neutral but actively reverting — which is precisely Greene's claim about strengths wearing down or turning into weaknesses without conscious effort.[^1]

**So two traditions, with no contact, converge on a non-obvious empirical claim: unmaintained good qualities do not plateau, they decay.** Greene reaches it from habit neurology; the sādhana corpus reached it from centuries of practitioners observing what happens when they stop.

And the contemplative side supplies something Greene's account is missing entirely, which is a **rate**. Greene says strengths need practice and does not say how much or how often. The japa material is specific, and the specificity is the useful part: **the question is not whether you are working on a quality but whether the frequency exceeds the decay rate**, and below that threshold effort produces nothing at all rather than a little.

Which reframes a common and demoralizing experience. People who work on a quality intermittently and observe no improvement usually conclude they lack aptitude. **The likelier explanation is that they have been practising below the maintenance threshold** — doing real work whose entire output is consumed keeping the trait from degrading, and mistaking the absence of progress for the absence of capacity.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication:** the resting state of an unattended character is not neutral. **It is the worst available version of itself**, arrived at by doing nothing — because the weak trait is the default path and defaults are free, while every strength is an override running on an attention budget that stress empties first. Which means there is no such thing as maintaining your standards; there is only paying for them, continuously, and noticing what disappears on the weeks you cannot.

**Generative questions:**

- If the decay is continuous and practice below a threshold only offsets it, then most self-improvement effort produces no visible gain while being genuinely necessary — and is indistinguishable, from inside, from wasted effort. **How would anyone tell the difference between a practice that is holding a trait steady and one that is doing nothing at all?**
- The one item on Greene's list that does not run on personal attention is proximity to strong characters.[^4] If environment beats intention under load, then character is substantially a property of who you are around — which is a claim about *company* rather than about persons, and it inverts the whole chapter's programme of evaluating individuals. Does the strong character you are trying to hire exist independently of the environment you would be removing them from?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/character-as-engraving|Character as Engraving]] — the laid-path mechanism from which this asymmetry follows

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/the-five-inflaming-factors|The Five Inflaming Factors]] — rising pressure as the condition that empties the override budget
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/joan-crawford-and-the-alchemy|Joan Crawford and the Alchemy]] — the alternative to maintenance: converting the weak trait into the strength
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/trait-development-composure-charisma|Trait Development: Composure and Charisma]] — the curriculum Greene's paragraph lacks
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/hours-not-minutes-the-discipline-of-japa|Hours Not Minutes: The Discipline of Japa]] — the same asymmetry, with a maintenance threshold attached

## Footnotes

[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/robert-greene-laws-of-human-nature|Greene, *The Laws of Human Nature*]] — l.1336. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` The full passage: strengths requiring awareness and practice; life weakening us; generosity without discrimination and confidence becoming grandiosity; "the weakest parts of our character are the ones that create habits and compulsive behavior, because they do not require effort or practice to maintain." 🚩 SINGLE SOURCE.
[^2]: Ibid., l.1332. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` The neurological engraving; "the path is already laid."
[^3]: Ibid., l.582–584. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` Stress revealing carefully concealed flaws; "Never imagine that you are someone who can withstand rising stress without emotional leakage."
[^4]: Ibid., l.1486–1488. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` The six cultivation practices; "the only way to do so is to work on your habits."
[^5]: Ibid., l.1408. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` Weak character neutralizing other qualities; the hidden costs; "People of real strength are as rare as gold."
[^6]: Ibid., l.1476–1484. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` Character as clay; the four worked conversions (hyperperfectionist, pleaser, hypersensitive, rebel); "For each weakness there is a corresponding strength."

# Writing Saturn Under Saturn: Method as Embodiment

## The Capture

Foss at Saturn S62: *"I am writing this with Saturn exactly transiting my Ascendant. It surely has been a blessing."*

One sentence. Inside a commentary on a different mantra. The disclosure looks small. It is methodological. Foss is telling the reader that he wrote the Saturn-volume under the operationally-most-relevant Saturn-transit possible: Saturn over his own first house, the placement that in standard chart-reading would predict the most pressure on identity, energy, and direction. The volume's content is therefore not lecture-notes from an outside observer; it is testimony from inside the graha he is documenting.

At R45 Foss confirms the pattern for Rāhu: *"I was writing the Rāhu chapter when Rāhu was in Aries."*

## The Live Wire

- **First wire (obvious)**: "Foss likes to disclose when his life mirrors what he's writing about."
- **Second wire (deeper)**: If Foss writes each volume under operationally-relevant transits of the graha being documented, then the entire 9-volume corpus is a meta-witness apparatus where the author embodies each graha while documenting it. The corpus is not a translation; it is a documented practice. This is a methodological-commitment no other Vedic-astrology corpus replicates at this level.
- **Third wire (uncomfortable)**: Reading the Foss corpus serially in the order of the graha-Dashās in one's own chart would deliver each volume during the period the volume is most operationally relevant to the reader. The 9 volumes become a 120-year reading-schedule (one Vimshottari-cycle) where each volume arrives at the time when the practitioner's own chart is most receptive to its content. Foss does not propose this reading-protocol explicitly. The architecture implies it.

## The Connection It Makes

Connects to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/foss-autobiographical-method-as-witness-all-four-outer-planet-volumes|Foss's Autobiographical Method as Witness page]] — S62 is the most-explicit instance.

**Essay seed**: "Method as Embodiment — When the Author Writes from Inside the Subject They Document." The Foss S62 disclosure as a case-study in practitioner-authorship that requires writing-from-inside the operational-conditions.

**Open question**: Were all 9 volumes written under operationally-relevant transits? Colophon-comparison across the print edition could test the pattern.

# The Outcome Test, Suspended Where Outcomes Are Worst

## The Moment

Strategy 30 hands you the hardest sentence in the book. Machiavelli's *verità effettuale*, transposed onto communication: judge by results, not intent. Communication that doesn't advance its cause or produce the desired result is just self-indulgent talk. And the follow-through, which is the part that stings — a failure to communicate is the fault of the unstrategic communicator, never of the dull-witted audience.

That's a real standard. It costs something to hold. It's on [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/the-effective-truth-standard|The Effective Truth Standard]].

Three chapters later, Strategy 33 needs to argue that terrorism works. And the standard goes out the window. Greene writes that it's a mistake to judge this kind of war by the rubric of victory or defeat, and offers instead *the ability to effect some kind of change*.

Every violent act effects some kind of change. There is no possible instance that fails that test. He set the hardest outcome standard in the volume and suspended it for the one chapter where the outcomes are worst.

## Why It Landed

`[RESONANCE]` Because it's the tell, and it's the only one of its kind in the book.

Everywhere else, the contradictions this ingest logged — twenty numbered, four more named on pages after the counter stopped — are two chapters wanting different things and neither noticing the other. Strategy 14 wants the initiative and Strategy 11 wants the opponent to overextend. Strategy 19 wants no hope left and Strategy 22 wants a settlement the loser can live with. Those are ordinary. A book of thirty-three separately argued positions will contradict itself and most readers will never hold two chapters in mind at once.

This one is different in kind. It isn't two positions colliding. It's a *criterion* being applied and then withdrawn, and the withdrawal happens precisely where applying it would produce an answer the chapter doesn't want. Run Strategy 30's standard on Strategy 33's material honestly and you have to price the deaths against what they bought, which is the arithmetic the chapter exists to avoid.

## The Structural Observation

The vault holds both ends and they're cross-linked — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/the-asymmetry-of-having-less-to-lose|The Asymmetry of Having Less to Lose]] names the suspension, [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/the-effective-truth-standard|The Effective Truth Standard]] holds the standard being suspended. So the connection is already on disk. What isn't yet developed is what the pattern predicts.

Because there's a second suspension, and it points the same way. Strategy 30's standard, applied to *the book itself*, is devastating and comfortable at the same time. By effective truth, *The 33 Strategies of War* is an unambiguous triumph — millions of copies, an enormous readership, decades of influence. The standard has no way to register that this ingest found its historical cases repeatedly altered, dates moved, an epidemic dropped from a conquest, a coalition that formed reported as a coalition avoided. Effective truth doesn't ask whether the material was accurate. That's not a loophole in the standard, it's the standard.

So the same criterion is a scalpel pointed outward and an anaesthetic pointed inward, and both uses are live inside one book.

And here's the part that makes this worth developing rather than just noting: Strategy 33 goes on to *supply* the honest answer and then not use it. The counter-doctrine at the end of that chapter — composure, intelligence work, don't overreact, an aggressive counterstrike is a sign of weakness, panic reveals the degree to which the enemy has already won — argues that terror's power is borrowed and revocable. That's the effective-truth verdict. Twenty paragraphs said the thing is nearly unbeatable; the last five say it only works if you let it. Greene doesn't reconcile them, and the second half is considerably better supported than the first.

## The Collision Candidate

Against [[LAB/Sparks/the-ambiguous-record-always-resolves-toward-design|The Ambiguous Record Always Resolves Toward Design]]. Both are cases of a standard the book holds sincerely in one place and relaxes wherever holding it would cost an argument. Together they're the beginning of an account of *where* a strategy book bends — not randomly, and not out of dishonesty, but at exactly the points where rigour would eliminate a chapter.

**Promotion criterion:** find the third instance. Two is a pair; three is a mechanism. The likeliest candidate is Strategy 25's closing advice to avoid wars of morality, delivered after a hundred and thirty lines teaching how to start one — check whether that's the same move (a standard applied and withdrawn) or merely the ordinary Reversal hedge Greene ends most chapters with.

## Status

- [x] Speculative
- [ ] Being developed
- [ ] Ready to promote

## Next action

Read Strategy 25's Reversal against Strategy 33's counter-doctrine section side by side and decide whether they're the same move. If they are, this merges with the design-bias spark into a single piece about where the book's rigour is load-bearing and where it's decorative.
